title: The Web Before TLS: Why HTTP Sucks 😱
description: Learn why HTTP without TLS is an eavesdropper’s paradise and what threats TLS solves.

slides.title: HTTP = Everything in Plain Sight 👁️
slides.content:
# Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) sends data as raw text across the network.

- No encryption – anyone on the same Wi‑Fi can read your passwords, credit cards, private messages.
- No authentication – you don’t know if the server is really your bank or a fake.
- No integrity – an attacker can modify the webpage or inject malware.

HTTP is like sending a postcard: the postman (and everyone at the sorting office) can read and modify it.

slides.title: The Three Amigos of TLS 🤠🤠🤠
slides.content:
# TLS (Transport Layer Security) adds three critical protections on top of TCP:

1. **Confidentiality** – Encryption prevents eavesdropping.
2. **Authentication** – The server (and optionally the client) proves its identity using certificates.
3. **Integrity** – A Message Authentication Code (MAC) prevents tampering.

Together, these turn the postcard into a locked, signed, tamper‑proof briefcase.

quizData.question: Which of these is NOT a protection provided by TLS?
quizData.explanation: TLS might slow things a bit due to encryption overhead, but does not inherently speed up loading. It provides security, not performance.

slides.title: A Brief History: SSL → TLS 📜
slides.content:
# SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) was created by Netscape in the 90s. TLS is its successor.

- SSL 1.0 – never released.
- SSL 2.0, 3.0 – both broken, now deprecated.
- TLS 1.0 (1999) – slight upgrade of SSL 3.0.
- TLS 1.1 – deprecated.
- TLS 1.2 (2008) – still widely used, secure if configured properly.
- TLS 1.3 (2018) – modern, simpler, faster, and more secure.

Today, “SSL” is often used as a generic term, but we mean TLS. Always use TLS 1.2 or 1.3.

slides.title: Plain HTTP – A Wiretap Demo
slides.content: Using curl to see the plaintext leakage (no encryption):
slides.codeSnippet:
# Capture network traffic on plain HTTP
curl -v http://example.com

# In the output, everything is visible: headers, HTML, cookies.
# With HTTPS (curl https://...), you'd see only encrypted binary.

slides.title: Always Check the Padlock 🔒
slides.content: ## Look for the padlock icon and `https://` in your browser. If it’s missing, assume everything you type or see can be intercepted. Never enter passwords on HTTP pages.

quizData.question: SSL 3.0 is still secure and recommended for modern servers.
quizData.explanation: False. SSL 3.0 is vulnerable to POODLE and other attacks, and has been deprecated for years.
